practice.title: Dedicating Every Virtue to Overcome Your Delusion
agreedSteps: After every virtuous action this week — meditating, being kind, doing the dishes — dedicate toward the elimination of your chosen delusion and for the benefit of all living beings.
Recognize opportunities to dedicate — catch yourself after positive actions and make the dedication, rather than letting them pass unnoticed.
steps: When dedicating, imagine what it would really look like and feel like to have a cessation of your chosen delusion. Don't settle for a generic image of 'peace' — try to picture the specific opponent mind, the reversal in your own life. What does the you-version of that freedom actually look like?

Use the Geshe Ben Gungyel method: tally a positive stone each time you remember to dedicate, and a dark stone when you realize you forgot. Make a prediction of the ratio beforehand and check it at the end of the week.

With the four specific dedications (general, for the sick, for hunger and thirst, to fulfill wishes), try to bring them alive by imagining the suffering of specific beings and then dedicating to become the answer to their prayers.
practice.quote: Every time we do something virtuous over this week ahead, let's start practicing this. [...] Doing the dishes, or being nice to this person, or meditating. Do this positive action. May I benefit all living beings, and especially through overcoming this specific delusion. And then when we dedicate, we imagine, what does that really look like?

commentary.title: Choose One Delusion and Focus
content: We're each picking one of the 26 delusions — six root delusions and twenty secondary delusions — to focus on and oppose over this period. As we move into the chapters on conscientiousness and guarding alertness, this is the kind of work we're doing: identifying delusions, understanding how they work, and destroying them. Conscientiousness is like the CEO of the whole Dharma practice — the part of the mind that's vigilant against delusions and marshaling all our mental factors to increase virtue.

The key is focus. If we don't have one delusion as a paradigm or example, our mind becomes too dispersed and unfocused. Nothing moves. But mastering how to conquer one delusion pretty much tracks to conquering any delusion — the principles transfer over, like learning a language. Once you've done a couple, you really get how to learn a language, and you can learn many more. If you've never done it, it's really tough.

If there's ambiguity about which to pick, choose one that feels appealing — one where there's joy and personal interest. Not from a moralistic heaviness of 'I'm supposed to,' but from that word 'fun.' What would be joyful to work on and see some progress on?

commentary.title: Imagining the Cessation of a Delusion
content: When we dedicate, we should imagine the result of the dedication: what does it really look like to have a cessation of our chosen delusion? This is a very interesting practice, because the generic image will be incredibly unclear for most delusions. The obvious answer is always 'peace' or 'freedom,' and that's somewhere on the spectrum, but it's leaving out everything in between.

Take miserliness as an example. What does the complete cessation of miserliness really look like? It's not just freedom — it's the presence of the opponent: a spontaneous mind of giving, fueled by a huge realization of love. It requires hugely reduced self-cherishing and self-grasping, because without that we feel like 'I'm losing and you're winning' every time we give. It requires understanding of karma, no possessiveness in the mind, and insight into emptiness.

We can get closer to that image by rejoicing in examples we've seen in others, and by picturing what it would look like in our own life — a specific scene where we've overcome that delusion. Like being tired at the end of a work day and someone asks for our time, and we feel genuine delight. As Geshe-la says in Ocean of Nectar, the hair stands up on the back of our neck because we're like, 'I'm going to get to give!' We're not aiming for perfection — just something better than yesterday's model.
commentary.quote: Can I get a mental image that's better than yesterday's mental image of what this would be like? Or at least something that moves my heart and excites me and delights me. Makes me feel really good inside.

commentary.title: The Four-Step Practice of Compassionate Dedication
content: The dedication for the sick is a very wonderful meditation that KK laid out as a four-step practice. Step one: empathize with people's pain — try to bring alive the suffering of those who are sick. Meditate on those confined to a hospital, those sick and dying alone without a friend to care for them, those whose tears we have seen and whose cries we have heard.

Step two: develop compassion on the basis of that empathy, that exchanging self with others. What is it really like from their point of view to be forgotten about in a home somewhere, getting treatment while no one comes to visit and the whole family doesn't want to bother anymore? Really feel into their perspective.

Step three: make a wish to protect that person. And step four: in our dedication, dedicate to actually become the answer to their prayers. We can imagine sending out countless emanations to be kind and loving doctors, nurses, support staff, friends, and medicine. We can imagine sending that out to all the hospitals in New York City and picture what it would be like to really be a healer for them.

This same four-step structure applies to all the specific dedications — for those suffering from hunger and thirst, for those needing refuge, for all those in need. As Bodhisattvas in training, we carry a special place in our heart for these beings.

commentary.title: Pain Becomes Our Strength as Healers
content: When we have an incredibly painful memory or experience that we haven't really moved on from yet, it becomes hard to encounter similitudes of that experience. The healing has two sides. One is exploring what that complete healing looks like, using the same imagination practice — what would it look like to reach that place of total healing? It's not saying we have to be there today, but it's really nice to start imagining that.

The other side is taking our pain and transmuting it into becoming a healer for others. When someone's a real healer, they usually heal the pain that they dealt with, and that pain gets transmuted into healing. The pain becomes a strength. It's a Lojong practice of transforming adversity. Then going into a difficult setting will have a very different feeling — we feel like a healer moving through that environment, with medicine blood at our heart. Our pain becomes our strength in those kinds of situations.

commentary.title: Cosmic Dedications — Thinking Big
content: The dedications for future ages — for those who will suffer during the aeon of famine, the aeon of weapons, and the destruction of the world system — are about extending our vision beyond this world and this realm. The Buddhas are like cosmic beings playing a game of chess over a millions-of-lifetime arc. They're setting up things to work over countless worlds and aeons.

These kind of dedications are incredibly pure because they're so utterly useless for the self-cherishing mind right now. We're never going to see the results. They have a kind of beauty and elegance to them — they're so pure-hearted. And the dedication to fulfill the wishes of sentient beings — praying to become whatever it might be that others require, an inexhaustible treasury, always at their disposal — concludes the first four of the five preparatory practices for accumulating merit.

commentary.title: Training the Mind in Giving
content: We should train our mind well now in the thought of giving up our body and possessions, because we'll have to give up everything we own at the time of death anyway. If we cling possessively to our body and wealth as we pass from this life, we will experience great inner torment and plant the seeds of a lower rebirth. To be able to give our body and possessions to others voluntarily is the best way to extract meaning from them.

A Bodhisattva who has gained a realization of exchanging self with others thinks 'I' on respect to all living beings. In their psychological experience, every being is as validly labeled as self or me. They have this mind that's at one with the whole of life. For that person, if sacrificing one body is the way to help the entire whole, they're like — sure, no problem. The Bodhisattva views the body like a tree, like a clod of earth. If someone's cutting it down, okay. If someone's anointing it with perfume, also okay. Both are met with equal love and compassion.

The Sadaprarudita story, previously read in class, demonstrates this incredible yearning for Dharma — a willingness to crack open his very marrow in exchange for teachings. That crystallized yearning is an incredibly useful image to think about: what would it be like for us to have that same yearning, especially in overcoming our specific delusion?
commentary.quote: I really, really want to [destroy this delusion]. Not like desperate in a kind of neurotic way, but we want to so much that we almost can't stop thinking about it. I really am kind of voraciously consuming all the tools I can get to uproot this delusion. I'm putting in the time and energy, I'm thinking about it. I'm taking everything I've got.

commentary.title: Dealing with Intrusive, Discouraged Thoughts
content: When doing positive meditation and intrusive thoughts come — 'What if this doesn't happen? You're lying to yourself. What if nothing changes?' — the approach is a very strict one. These thoughts aren't based in any evaluation of how we're actually doing. They're just discouraged, self-attacking thoughts from creepy-crawly delusions lurking in the mind. If we improve, they'll always keep attacking. They're not evaluating us — they're just there to bring us down.

The practice is to treat them like an evil minister in the boardroom of our mind. Every time they talk, we don't listen at all. We don't try to placate them, and we don't try to disprove them — because that's taking them seriously, and they don't deserve to be taken seriously. We treat them like static, like noise on the wrong radio signal.

The phrase to use like a sword: 'This is just a thought.' We stab through those Mara thoughts with it. This is just a thought. I'm not going to give it any energy. Over time, we'll start to notice them very clearly — oh, those are just nonsense thoughts. They're from the delusions. I don't need to make them better. I need to ignore them 100%.

commentary.title: Dedication as a Power Tool — KK's Example
content: How do we know if dedication is working? With long-term karmic effects, there's always a lag — it's hard to get a proper signal right away. Sometimes we see a gradual lessening. Sometimes it's very stark. When dedicating to stop drinking, after a month of doing it every day with every virtuous action — wanted to, wanted to, wanted to, no lessening — and then one morning, no interest. Poof. Vanished.

If we notice something isn't changing at all, it's usually not a sign that our dedication is the problem. It's a sign that we're creating more of the karma we're trying to dedicate to undo, or we're not dealing with the delusions that lead to that experience. If we're dedicating for a better relationship but constantly fueling anger in every other area of our life, that sweet little dedication is going up against a tidal wave going the other direction.

dataShares.speaker: Ryan
dataShares.summary: Noticed that certain people and certain questions trigger him — being asked about attending specific classes caused him to lash out. Investigating why certain topics cause anger. In the meditation, couldn't connect with the guru dissolution practice, so shifted to enjoying the company of the sangha — his heart dissolved with the sangha rather than with gurus.

dataShares.speaker: Mimi
dataShares.summary: Reflecting on Kadam Morton's teaching at NEDC about being a 'fortunate assembly' and how Buddha Shakyamuni created the karma for that gathering. Connected it to what TTP is studying about turning the wheel of Dharma and beseeching the Buddhas not to pass away. The whole thing came alive in her heart.

dataShares.speaker: Anne
dataShares.summary: Discovered the practice of reducing self-cherishing in a very practical way. Whenever a problem came up, she reminded herself she's one of eight billion people, and then turned her mind to three specific people she knew who had bigger problems. It saved enormous mental energy and smoothed things out remarkably, especially during a challenging week.

dataShares.speaker: Marianne
dataShares.summary: At NEDC, after five days in bed she wanted to attend the last session but a communication problem prevented her. Got super deluded and angry. Suzanne helped her see it clearly — it wasn't personal. Recognized this as the same karma of abandonment she's been purifying all year. Saw it as part of the path: 'This karma hasn't been purified yet, but it might be on its way.'

dataShares.speaker: Kristin
dataShares.summary: Main NEDC takeaways: gratitude for everyone who helped put it on, the theme of having fun while practicing Dharma (if you're not having fun, you're not practicing Dharma), and a deeper insight into the Liberating Prayer — that happiness comes directly from blessings and indirectly from virtuous activities, because a blessing transforms the mind from negative to positive.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Grateful for her faith — even when struggling, she clings to the fact that she believes. Two NEDC reminders: the Liberating Prayer line about Buddha having done all the work through his compassionate intention and blessings, and the teaching that Geshe-la has walked the path and we just have to follow in his footsteps.

dataShares.speaker: David
dataShares.summary: Explored dependent relationship through role-switching: at a friend's wedding near his in-laws in Ohio, bouncing between family and friend contexts was disorienting. Same thing happened in Brooklyn when sangha friends and overseas colleagues mixed and then his wife arrived. Saw clearly that none of the individual roles is the real me, but without any of them there's nothing left — a practical emptiness meditation through roles.
